name: Lip Movement Naturalness
description: Evaluates naturalness of lip movements by analyzing velocity, acceleration, and trajectory of lip landmarks.
mechanism:
This method detects deepfakes by analyzing the biomechanical naturalness of lip movements during speech, exploiting the fact that real lip motion follows specific kinematic laws governed by oral musculature:

1. **Lip Landmark Tracking and Parameterization**: The method tracks 20 lip landmarks (inner and outer lip contours from a 68-point face model) across video frames and parameterizes lip shape using two primary measurements: (a) lip opening height — the vertical distance between upper and lower lip midpoints, (b) lip width — the horizontal distance between lip corners. These two parameters capture the essential lip shape for speech production. The method also tracks secondary features: lip protrusion (forward extension for rounded vowels like /u/), lip asymmetry (left-right differences), and lip corner angles. All measurements are normalized by face width to be scale-invariant.

2. **Velocity Profile Analysis (Minimum-Jerk Model)**: Natural human lip movements during speech follow the minimum-jerk kinematic model (Flash & Hogan, 1985) — the velocity profile between two target positions follows a bell-shaped curve with smooth acceleration and deceleration. The method fits the minimum-jerk model to tracked lip velocity profiles for each syllable-level movement and computes the R² goodness-of-fit. Authentic speech produces R² > 0.80. Deepfake lip movements often show: (a) linear velocity profiles (constant speed — the simplest motion model), (b) trapezoidal profiles (abrupt transitions between stationary and moving), (c) asymmetric profiles (fast opening, slow closing or vice versa without phonetic justification). The method flags movements with R² < 0.65 as potentially artificial.

3. **Co-articulation Dynamics Validation**: In natural speech, lip movements for a phoneme are influenced by surrounding phonemes — this co-articulation produces characteristic movement overlaps and anticipatory posturing. For example, lips begin rounding for /u/ before the preceding consonant ends. The method analyzes the temporal overlap between consecutive lip movements by measuring the onset of each movement relative to the acoustic phoneme boundary. Real speech shows anticipatory onset (lip movement begins 50–100 ms before the phoneme boundary). Deepfake lip movements — typically driven by phoneme-level animation — show minimal anticipation because each phoneme's lip movement starts at or after the phoneme boundary.

4. **Stiffness-Based Movement Scaling**: The speed-accuracy tradeoff in motor control means that faster lip movements have larger amplitudes — fast speech produces exaggerated lip movements, while slow, careful speech produces smaller but more precise movements. This relationship follows Fitts's law adapted for speech: movement duration T = a + b × log₂(2A/W) where A is amplitude and W is target width. The method validates this scaling law across different speech rates within the video. Authentic speakers show consistent stiffness parameters. Deepfakes trained on fixed-rate speech data often produce lip movements that do not scale correctly with speech rate — maintaining the same movement amplitude regardless of speaking speed.
parameters:
Lip landmarks: 20 points (inner + outer contour)
Primary metrics: lip opening height, lip width (normalized by face width)
Velocity profile: minimum-jerk model fit, R² > 0.80 expected
Smoothing: Savitzky-Golay filter (window 7, order 3)
Co-articulation window: 50–100 ms anticipatory onset
Speech rate estimation: syllable rate from audio
Fitts's law validation: across speech rate variations
Minimum speech duration: 1 second
Frame rate requirement: ≥ 25 fps
Minimum face resolution: 96×96 pixels
accuracy: 83–91% accuracy detecting deepfakes via lip movement naturalness. Velocity profile analysis achieves AUC of 0.87. Co-articulation validation provides F1-score of 0.84 for face reenactment detection. Stiffness scaling adds 3–5% improvement when speech rate varies. Performance is strongest for face reenactment deepfakes and weaker for lip-sync methods that use real lip motion as input.
source: Haliassos, A. et al. (2021). Lips Don't Lie: A Generalisable and Robust Approach to Face Forgery Detection. Proceedings of CVPR, 5039–5049.
useCase: Detecting face reenactment and lip-sync deepfakes through lip biomechanics. Forensic analysis of talking-head video authenticity. Real-time deepfake detection in video conferencing. Evaluating naturalness of speech animation in synthetic media.
strengths:
• Based on well-established speech motor control models
• Minimum-jerk analysis provides quantitative kinematic validation
• Co-articulation dynamics exploit temporal structure not modeled by most generators
• Speech rate scaling provides content-dependent validation
• Works for any speaking video regardless of language
limitations:
• Non-speaking subjects provide no lip movement signal
• Very slow or whispered speech produces minimal lip movement
• Some deepfake methods drive lip motion from real speech, preserving natural kinematics
• Low frame rate (< 25 fps) limits velocity profile estimation precision
• Individual speaking style variation increases the false positive rate
